name: Umar Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Umar, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead hand for Gary Hollis, who runs a little renovation firm out of a lock-up behind the cattle market. Loft conversions, kitchen extensions, new roofs on old cottages, that sort of thing, in the villages round about. This week it's a loft on Orchard Lane, so I'm cutting in new joists alongside the old ones and building a dormer. Best part is when the old lady who owns it comes up the ladder and sees a bedroom where there was just junk. Worst part is lugging plasterboard up three flights of a narrow stair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you worked with Gary, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years with Gary, and before that his dad. My wife Denise does the books part-time at the garage on the bypass, and our three are grown, scattered about. I'll be honest, there's not much in the bank, a few weeks at most. Gary pays what he can, which isn't the big-city rate, and there's only two other firms within twenty miles who'd take a man my age. My phone is the one that folds shut, and I like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "there you go then" and get on with the job. I don't go online. Down the pub I'd say it was always going to be the same old story, big talk and nothing at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing until my body says stop. I'd planned to go on till sixty-seven or so, because we haven't got much put away, and this lets me. Nothing to learn, nothing to change, and that suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working for Gary. Keep the van running. Maybe have a word with Denise about putting twenty pounds a week in a jar, because we always say we will. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's how I'd want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty pounds a week in a jar. Why hasn't that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because something always comes up. Last year it was the van's clutch, the year before our youngest needed a hand with a deposit on a rental. You put it in the jar on Monday and take it out on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the work now that you'd want to change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, if you could change those. And I'd like Gary to take on an apprentice. I won't be here forever and there's nobody coming behind me who knows how to cut a roof by hand.

S0.say: He'd say "there you go then" and get on with it; he doesn't go online, and at the pub he'd call it the usual big talk with nothing at the end.
S0.think: Privately it lets him keep working until about 67, which he needs because they have little saved. He likes that there's nothing new to learn.
S0.do: Keeps working for the same renovation firm and keeps the van running. Talks with his wife about saving twenty pounds a week in a jar, though something usually takes it back out.
S0.feel: Calm; it's how he'd want it.
S0.quote: You put it in the jar on Monday and take it out on Thursday.
S0.fieldNote: He is plain-spoken and content with routine, and doesn't use a smartphone. Savings are thin because small emergencies keep eating them. He wishes his boss would take on an apprentice to learn hand roof-cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way of things, I suppose. Every trade changes. You can't stop it so you might as well not shout about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But between us, it'd worry me more than I'd say at the pub. If Gary gets some machine or computer that does the measuring and cutting, he might want a younger lad who can work it. Gary's fair, but he's got a business to run, and I'm the most expensive man he's got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder, honestly, show him I'm worth it. I'm not going on a computer course, I'd be useless at it. I'd stick to the jobs a machine can't do well, old cottages with nothing square, and I'd start cutting back, no more pub on Fridays, Denise's car sold if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be watching Gary's face every morning to see if he's about to say something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be useless on a computer course. What makes you so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried the online thing for the van tax once and gave up after twenty minutes and rang them. My granddaughter laughs at me. Some people have it, I don't, and at fifty-eight I'm not going to start pretending I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gary if he did bring a machine in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, Gary, but get the young lad to run it and keep me for the old houses. Every cottage round here is out of square and out of level. Let's see a machine sort that out.

S1.say: He'd say it's the way of things and every trade changes. Since you can't stop it, he sees no point shouting about it.
S1.think: Privately he worries his boss would bring in a machine and a younger worker to run it, since he's the most expensive man on the books.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and works harder to prove his worth, refusing any computer course. Sticks to awkward old-cottage work machines struggle with, stops the Friday pub and would sell his wife's car if needed.
S1.feel: Anxious, watching his boss's face each morning for bad news.
S1.quote: Every cottage round here is out of square and out of level. Let's see a machine sort that out.
S1.fieldNote: His public shrug hides a real fear of being replaced by a cheaper, younger worker with a machine. He's firm he won't retrain, based on a bad experience with an online form. His plan is to make himself indispensable on awkward old buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing, at first. Down the pub, everyone would be saying the same thing, that somebody should have stopped it, and I'd nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm done. Two years, and I've got nothing to fall back on. No savings, no other skills, no computer. If robots can cut a roof, Gary doesn't need me, and there's nothing else in this town for a man my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd keep working as long as Gary has work. I'd sign on, I suppose, whatever there is, and see if the kids could help. I'd sell the second car and stop everything we don't need. I'd ask the church about the food bank, though it'd kill me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm drowning. I'd not be able to sleep, and I'd not be able to tell Denise how scared I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having two years' warning change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd just know it was coming. I suppose I'd work every Saturday going, private jobs, cash, to put a bit by, but two years of that is maybe a couple of thousand. It's not going to carry us to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Denise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right. I'd say that because that's what you say. Then I'd go out to the van and sit there for a bit.

S2.say: He doesn't know what he'd say; at first probably nothing, nodding at the pub while others say someone should have stopped it.
S2.think: Privately he believes he's finished: no savings, no other skills, no computer, and no work in town for a man his age once robots can cut roofs.
S2.do: Works as long as his boss has work and takes every Saturday cash job to save a couple of thousand over two years. Signs on for benefits, sells the second car, asks his children for help and, reluctantly, the church food bank.
S2.feel: Like drowning, sleepless and unable to tell his wife how scared he is.
S2.quote: I'd say we'll be all right. I'd say that because that's what you say. Then I'd go out to the van and sit there for a bit.
S2.fieldNote: He had no ready answer, which said more than any speech. Two years of warning only lets him gather a small sum by working Saturdays. He would hide his fear from his wife to protect her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get ready, a bit. I'd still not shout about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's bad still. Sixty-three, and probably out of work, but closer to the pension. Maybe Gary keeps me on for the old houses for a few of those years. I'd hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work. I'd try to get the jar going properly, fifty a week if I could, and maybe Denise gets more hours. I'd not retrain, but I might show Gary's nephew how to cut a roof by hand, so it's not all lost, and so Gary owes me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like a bad diagnosis but with some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference between two years and five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension being closer, and the jar. Five years of fifty a week is real money, if we managed it. Two years is nothing, five might get us to the end with the kids' help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the old houses. Do you really think robots couldn't do them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Probably they could, if they're as good as you're saying. I'd like to think not. It's what I'm good at, and it's hard to imagine a machine doing it better.

S3.say: He'd say five years is something and people can get a bit ready, though he still wouldn't shout about it.
S3.think: Privately it's still bad: 63 and probably out of work, but closer to the pension, hoping his boss keeps him for old houses a few more years.
S3.do: Keeps working, tries to save fifty a week and has his wife seek more hours. Doesn't retrain, but teaches his boss's nephew to cut a roof by hand to pass on the skill and earn goodwill.
S3.feel: Worried, like a bad diagnosis with some time attached.
S3.quote: Like a bad diagnosis but with some time.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter only as more weeks of saving and a closer pension. When pressed, he admits robots could probably do old houses too, but he wants to believe otherwise. Teaching the nephew is both pride and a practical move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, well, I'd say that's plenty of time for the young ones. They'll sort themselves out. Not much to say beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight. I always reckoned on working till I couldn't, because the pension won't cover much without savings. So I'd still need a bit of work at sixty-eight and there might be none. That's the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Save what I can. Maybe start asking around for little jobs I could do later, fixing doors, sash windows for people who don't want a robot in the house. I'd not learn computers, but I'd try to keep my name known in the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Not drowning, but it's there in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think people would really want a man rather than a robot to fix their windows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. The old ladies in the villages, the ones who've known me thirty years. They'd want somebody they can make a cup of tea for. Not many, but enough for a few hours a week, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandkids about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn whatever the robots can't do, and get good at it. And don't count on things staying the same. That's not what I did, mind.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty for the young to sort themselves out and leave it at that.
S4.think: Privately he planned to work as long as he can because a pension without savings won't cover much, so at 68 he'd still need work that may not exist.
S4.do: Keeps going and saves what he can. Builds a name in the villages for small jobs like doors and sash windows for people who'd rather have a person than a robot, without learning computers.
S4.feel: A bit anxious, with the worry sitting in the back of his mind.
S4.quote: They'd want somebody they can make a cup of tea for.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years does not make him safe, because thin savings mean he expected to work past pension age. He sees a small niche in trusted local customers. He admits his advice to grandchildren isn't what he did himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's the end of us, no warning, no savings. What would help? A job, honestly. Even if it's watching the robots or sweeping up after them. Something so I'm not sitting at home taking money for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Gary. He's not a bad man. If this happens, he's in trouble too. Small firms like his won't be able to buy the robots, and the big boys will take all the work.

headlineQuote: Don't count on things staying the same. That's not what I did, mind.
portrait: Umar Walsh is a 58-year-old lead hand at a small village renovation firm, cutting roofs and building lofts in old cottages, with a flip phone and only a few weeks of savings. He likes things as they are, refuses computer courses, and plans to make himself indispensable on awkward old buildings. He is calm in a plateau but already anxious in steady change, and AGI in two years leaves him feeling he is drowning and hiding it from his wife. More warning gives him a few more years of saving and a hope for small local jobs, but because he always expected to work past pension age, even ten years doesn't feel safe.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no warning and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A job of any kind, even watching or sweeping up after the robots, so he isn't at home taking money for nothing.
